steps.summary: All 4 species can be read, the roles make an experiment and the conditions are physical.
details: Species: Ag+(aq): reactant, silver ion; Cl-(aq): reactant, chloride ion; AgCl(s): product, silver chloride; H2O(l): solvent, water.
Conditions: 298.15 K, 1 bar, 60 s, environment aqueous-solution.

steps.title: Check conservation of atoms and charge
steps.summary: Balanced with the smallest whole-number coefficients: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s).
details: Atoms on the reactant side and on the product side: Ag 1 = 1, Cl 1 = 1.
Charge on the reactant side and on the product side: 0 = 0.
Balancing is bookkeeping: it shows that the equation is possible, not that the reaction takes place.

steps.title: Select the models that apply
steps.summary: Thermodynamics is selected; no sourced rate law exists for this reaction, so its kinetics is not simulated.
details: Stoichiometry: applies. The equation is balanced.
Thermodynamics: selected. Standard reaction enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant from the reference table, as far as the table covers the species.
Kinetics: not available. No sourced rate law exists for this reaction, and the rate law of a similar reaction is never substituted.

steps.title: Look up the reference data
steps.summary: Every species of the equation is in the reference table.
details: Ag+(aq): silver ion (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics); ΔfH° = 105.79 ± 0.08 kJ/mol; S° = 73.45 ± 0.40 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
Cl-(aq): chloride ion (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics); ΔfH° = −167.080 ± 0.10 kJ/mol; S° = 56.60 ± 0.20 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.
AgCl(s): silver chloride (CODATA Key Values for Thermodynamics); ΔfH° = −127.01 ± 0.05 kJ/mol; S° = 96.25 ± 0.20 J/(mol K), as printed by the source.

steps.title: Name the calculation engine
steps.summary: Engines used: exact rational balancing and Hess's law on reference values.
details: Balancing: exact rational null space of the element-and-charge composition matrix, scaled to the smallest whole numbers; no floating-point arithmetic.

Thermodynamics: Hess's law on the tabulated standard enthalpies of formation and standard entropies at 298.15 K; ΔG°(T) = ΔH°(298.15 K) − T·ΔS°(298.15 K) with the reaction enthalpy and entropy taken as independent of temperature; K = exp(−ΔG°/RT); uncertainties of the table values combined in quadrature.
Engine: @matterlab/reactions 0.1.0. It is deterministic: no clock and no random numbers are used.

steps.title: Run the calculation
steps.summary: Calculated: thermodynamic values from the reference table.
details: Reaction enthalpy ΔrH°(298.15 K) = −65.72 ± 0.14 kJ/mol; reaction entropy ΔrS°(298.15 K) = −33.80 ± 0.49 J/(mol K).
With every species in its standard state the reaction is product-favoured.
Thermodynamics: closed-form sums over table values; there is nothing to converge.

steps.title: State the limitations
steps.summary: 5 limitations apply, 1 of them because of this particular experiment.
details: MATTER LAB did not predict this reaction: it evaluated the equation built from the species that were entered. A balanced equation is bookkeeping, not evidence that the reaction takes place.

Catalysts and solvents are recorded with the experiment but not modelled: no supported model describes catalysis or solvation, so the results are those of the reaction as written. Recorded: H2O(l) (solvent).

Thermodynamic values refer to every species in its standard state (pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, ideal solutes). They are not the values of an actual mixture, and no equilibrium composition is computed.
A favourable Gibbs energy says nothing about rate: thermodynamics tells where the equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached or whether the reaction starts at all without ignition or a catalyst.
No sourced rate law is available for this reaction, so nothing is said about how fast it is. MATTER LAB does not substitute the rate law of a similar reaction.

assumptions: All species are in their standard states: pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, and aqueous species in the solute standard state of the source table.

Reaction enthalpy and entropy follow from Hess's law: the sum over products minus the sum over reactants of the tabulated enthalpies of formation and standard entropies at 298.15 K, each multiplied by its coefficient.
Aqueous ions follow the convention of the source table, in which H+(aq) has an enthalpy of formation of 0 and an entropy of 0; single-ion values are meaningful only in charge-balanced combinations.
Uncertainties are the limits printed by the sources, combined in quadrature as if they were independent; correlations between tabulated values are not known to this package.
The Gibbs energy is ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° at 298.15 K, the temperature of the tabulated data.
K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) is the dimensionless thermodynamic equilibrium constant, expressed in activities relative to the standard states above.

beginner.heading: What this experiment asks
paragraphs: This experiment looks at the reaction **Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s)**.
It asks how much heat the reaction gives out or takes in and which side of the reaction is favoured.
MATTER LAB works on the reaction you entered. It does not decide whether these substances really react.

beginner.heading: What goes in
paragraphs: Starting substances: silver ion (Ag+, aqueous solution) and chloride ion (Cl-, aqueous solution). Products entered: silver chloride (AgCl, solid).
Also listed: water (H2O, liquid) as solvent.
Temperature 298.15 K (25 °C), pressure 1 bar.

beginner.heading: How it was worked out
paragraphs: First the equation was balanced, so that no atoms and no electric charge appear or disappear.
Then published reference values for each substance were added up, products minus starting substances. This is known as Hess's law. Nothing was simulated for it.
No speed was worked out: MATTER LAB has no published rate data for this reaction and does not borrow data from a similar one.

beginner.heading: The idea behind the numbers: energy
paragraphs: The heat of reaction, written ΔH, is the heat content of the products minus that of the starting substances. A negative value means that heat is given out.
Whether a reaction is favoured depends on that heat and on the change in disorder (the entropy, ΔS). The two are combined in the Gibbs energy ΔG. A negative ΔG means that the products are favoured.

beginner.heading: What is assumed
paragraphs: Every substance is treated as pure and under standard conditions (a pressure of 1 bar).

beginner.heading: What came out
paragraphs: Balanced equation: **Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s)**.
Heat of reaction: **−65.72 ± 0.14 kJ/mol** for the amounts in the equation, counted in moles. The minus sign means that heat is **given out** (the reaction is exothermic).
Gibbs energy at 298.15 K: **−55.64 ± 0.20 kJ/mol**. The products are favoured.
Equilibrium constant: K ≈ 5.6 × 10⁹. The larger this number, the further the balance lies towards the products.

beginner.heading: How sure is this
paragraphs: The balanced equation is exact arithmetic; its numbers are certain.
The ± values come from the uncertainties given in the reference tables.
These numbers carry the label "Computed": Produced by a real calculation. The method, settings and limitations are recorded.
Numbers are rounded so that they show no more digits than the data behind them support.

beginner.heading: Did the calculation finish
paragraphs: These results are exact arithmetic and sums of table values. There is no step-by-step calculation that could fail to finish.

beginner.heading: What is not included
paragraphs: MATTER LAB did not predict that these substances react. It only did the sums for the reaction you entered.
H2O(l) (solvent) is noted down but not part of the calculation. The results are for the reaction exactly as written.
The energy values are for pure substances under standard conditions, not for a real mixture.
Being favoured is not the same as being fast. A favoured reaction can be far too slow to notice, or may need a spark to start.
MATTER LAB has no published speed data for this reaction, so it says nothing about how fast it goes.

beginner.heading: Why reality may differ
paragraphs: Real mixtures are not under standard conditions: the actual pressures and concentrations shift the balance.
A favoured reaction can still be so slow that nothing visible happens, or it may need a spark or a catalyst to start.
The reaction that really happens may not be the one written down: other products can form.

advanced.heading: Objective
paragraphs: Evaluate the reaction Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s) at 298.15 K and 1 bar: the balanced equation, the standard reaction enthalpy, entropy, Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant from reference data and the rate constant and concentration-time curves, if a sourced rate law exists for exactly this reaction.
Method requested: auto. The equation was built from the species entered as reactants and products; no product was predicted.

advanced.heading: Mathematical model: conservation
paragraphs: The coefficients ν (negative for reactants, positive for products) have to satisfy the conservation equations for every element and for the charge.
These equations have a single solution up to scale here; the smallest positive whole numbers are used.
advanced.equation: Σ ν·(atoms of each element) = 0,  Σ ν·(charge) = 0

advanced.heading: Mathematical model: reaction enthalpy and entropy
paragraphs: Hess's law: the standard reaction enthalpy and entropy at 298.15 K are the stoichiometric sums of the tabulated standard enthalpies of formation and standard entropies.
advanced.equation: ΔrH° = Σ ν·ΔfH°,  ΔrS° = Σ ν·S°

paragraphs: The standard Gibbs energy of reaction at 298.15 K follows from the reaction enthalpy and entropy, and the thermodynamic equilibrium constant from the Gibbs energy.

advanced.heading: Assumptions
paragraphs: All species are in their standard states: pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, and aqueous species in the solute standard state of the source table.

Reaction enthalpy and entropy follow from Hess's law: the sum over products minus the sum over reactants of the tabulated enthalpies of formation and standard entropies at 298.15 K, each multiplied by its coefficient.

Uncertainties are the limits printed by the sources, combined in quadrature as if they were independent; correlations between tabulated values are not known to this package.
The Gibbs energy is ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° at 298.15 K, the temperature of the tabulated data.
K = exp(−ΔG°/RT) is the dimensionless thermodynamic equilibrium constant, expressed in activities relative to the standard states above.

The direction label compares ΔG° with RT and with its own uncertainty; it describes all species in their standard states, not an arbitrary mixture, and says nothing about how fast the reaction is or whether it proceeds at all.
Catalysts and solvents take no part in any of the models.

advanced.heading: Results
paragraphs: Balanced equation: Ag+(aq) + Cl-(aq) -> AgCl(s).
ΔrH°(298.15 K) = −65.72 ± 0.14 kJ/mol, per mole of reaction as written.
Direction with every species in its standard state: product-favoured.
No kinetic results: no sourced rate law exists for this reaction.

advanced.heading: Confidence and uncertainty
paragraphs: Stoichiometric coefficients are exact (rational arithmetic).

Uncertainties are the limits printed by the sources, combined in quadrature as independent quantities; correlations between tabulated values are unknown. The CODATA table gives "stated uncertainty limits" without a coverage factor.
Evidence: reaction enthalpy and entropy are computed from reference data; the Gibbs energy and equilibrium constant are labelled computed.
The reaction enthalpy is rounded to the second significant figure of its uncertainty.
The reaction entropy and the Gibbs energy are rounded to the second significant figure of their uncertainties.
The equilibrium constant is given with the digits that the uncertainty of the Gibbs energy supports (log10 K is uncertain by about 0.04).
A value that has an uncertainty is rounded, together with that uncertainty, to the decimal place of the second significant figure of the uncertainty.

advanced.heading: Convergence status
paragraphs: Balancing: exact, nothing to converge.
Thermodynamics: closed-form sums over table values, nothing to converge.

advanced.heading: Known limitations
paragraphs: MATTER LAB did not predict this reaction: it evaluated the equation built from the species that were entered. A balanced equation is bookkeeping, not evidence that the reaction takes place.

Catalysts and solvents are recorded with the experiment but not modelled: no supported model describes catalysis or solvation, so the results are those of the reaction as written. Recorded: H2O(l) (solvent).

Thermodynamic values refer to every species in its standard state (pure solids and liquids, ideal gases at 1 bar, ideal solutes). They are not the values of an actual mixture, and no equilibrium composition is computed.
A favourable Gibbs energy says nothing about rate: thermodynamics tells where the equilibrium lies, not how fast it is reached or whether the reaction starts at all without ignition or a catalyst.
No sourced rate law is available for this reaction, so nothing is said about how fast it is. MATTER LAB does not substitute the rate law of a similar reaction.

advanced.heading: Why the prediction may not match reality
paragraphs: The equation as written may not be the reaction that occurs: side reactions, incomplete conversion and other products are not considered.
Composition and non-ideality: the driving force in an actual mixture is ΔG = ΔG° + RT ln Q with activities that differ from the standard states; neither Q nor activity coefficients are computed.
Kinetic hindrance: thermodynamics implies nothing about rate, and metastable mixtures are common.
Reference data: tabulated values carry their own uncertainties and, where two tables are combined, need not be mutually consistent.
